question: Can surprise-triggered temperature control plus a count-based novelty bonus make an online agent adapt better to changing rewards, and does a quantum superposition-and-collapse analogy add a distinct algorithmic contribution?

key_findings.claim: The operational 'Free Will Equation' is a classical softmax exploration rule, not a quantum field model.
key_findings.evidence: Action probabilities are softmax of Q(s,a) plus alpha times an intrinsic bonus, divided by a temperature. The proposed bonus is 1/sqrt(1+N(s,a)), and temperature is multiplied up after a reward-surprise threshold and decayed otherwise. The paper explicitly says no quantum computation or physical quantum process is required.

key_findings.claim: The proposed ingredients substantially overlap established count-based intrinsic reward, adaptive entropy control, and non-stationary bandit restart methods.
key_findings.evidence: The paper itself describes epsilon-greedy, Boltzmann policies, entropy bonuses, count-based exploration, novelty search, and change-triggered re-annealing as direct analogues. Its claimed difference is the narrative unification and feedback-driven temperature, rather than a new estimator or decision-theoretic objective.

key_findings.claim: The first four-arm experiment gives the adaptive agent privileged knowledge of the change point, so it cannot validate autonomous surprise detection.
key_findings.evidence: At step 1,000, the adaptive agent is explicitly notified of the environmental change and its exploration rate is reset. The text acknowledges that an actual agent would need a statistical reward-change detector, but removes that problem 'for clarity.' The baseline receives no matched restart or oracle signal.

key_findings.claim: The printed ten-arm implementation does not learn a persistent bandit value for either agent because time is used as the dictionary state key.
key_findings.evidence: At each time t, the baseline selects argmax Q_base[t] and updates only Q_base[t], then moves to the never-seen Q_base[t+1]. The FreeWillAgent likewise evaluates Q[t], N[t], updates them once, and then acts from fresh Q[t+1], N[t+1]. Thus the displayed code makes its softmax uniform at each new step and prevents value or count accumulation across the stationary bandit state.

key_findings.claim: The printed ten-arm reward construction contradicts the stated optimal-arm switch.
key_findings.evidence: Before the switch, linspace(0.1,0.8,10) is followed by setting the last arm to 0.2, so arm 8, not arm 9, has the maximum probability. After reversing the array and setting arm 0 to 0.2, arm 1, not arm 0, is maximal. This undermines the accompanying description of an arm-9-to-arm-0 change.

key_findings.claim: The reported plots show higher post-change reward, policy divergence, and early action coverage for the labeled adaptive agent, but those plots are not valid evidence for the proposed learning mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: The four-arm narrative reports recovery to about 0.7 by step 1,200 and an entropy spike to about 1.5 bits. The ten-arm figures average ten seeds and display reward, KL divergence, and novelty. However, the oracle reset, unmatched baseline, fresh-state bug, and misidentified optimal arms mean the observed differences cannot be causally assigned to surprise-adaptive intrinsic exploration.

key_findings.claim: The paper does not support claims about AGI creativity, autonomy, or quantum advantage.
key_findings.evidence: All evaluation is on small Bernoulli bandits; no planning, language generation, creativity, high-dimensional state, continual learning, or quantum hardware task is tested. The limitations acknowledge simplistic environments, trigger-design difficulty, added hyperparameters, over-exploration risk, and pseudorandom rather than metaphysical freedom.

method.core_idea: Represent action propensities as a metaphorical superposition, sample an action through a softmax collapse, and adapt exploration using count-based novelty and reward surprise.
method.mechanism: The agent maintains Q values and action counts. It adds an inverse-square-root count bonus to action scores, samples from a softmax, and increases a bounded temperature when instantaneous reward deviates sufficiently from a moving average; otherwise the temperature decays. A separate experimental implementation also resets epsilon exactly at a known change point. The quantum terminology maps action basis vectors to a Hilbert space, probability sampling to collapse, and ordinary learning updates to state evolution, without using amplitudes, interference, complex phases, unitary dynamics, or quantum hardware.
assumptions: Reward deviation from a short moving average reliably indicates environmental non-stationarity rather than observation noise.
A single global temperature is an adequate control variable for exploration across states and actions.
Inverse-square-root action counts represent useful novelty in contextual or high-dimensional problems.
The intrinsic bonus and temperature update can be tuned without destabilizing external reward learning.
A decaying epsilon-greedy agent is the relevant baseline for adaptive non-stationary decision making.
Quantum vocabulary contributes explanatory or design value beyond classical stochastic policies.
Bandit adaptation results can meaningfully motivate AGI-level creativity and autonomy claims.

techniques.role: Favors actions with lower recorded visitation using 1/sqrt(1+N).
Raises policy entropy after a thresholded reward deviation and anneals it otherwise.
Combines estimated external value and intrinsic novelty into a stochastic policy.
Uses deviation from recent mean reward as a simple change signal.
Resets epsilon in the demonstration exactly when the environment switches.
Re-labels a classical action distribution and sample as a field superposition and collapse.

evaluations.setting: Four-armed Bernoulli bandit with one abrupt optimal-arm switch at step 1,000.
evaluations.metric: Rolling reward and policy entropy over time.
evaluations.result: The paper reports adaptive-agent reward recovering to about 0.7 by step 1,200 and entropy spiking near 1.5 bits after the switch.
evaluations.baseline: Monotonically decaying epsilon-greedy agent without the adaptive agent's oracle change notification.

evaluations.setting: Printed ten-arm, 2,000-step simulation over ten random seeds with a nominal switch at step 1,000.
evaluations.metric: 50-step rolling reward, KL divergence from the baseline policy, and cumulative fraction of distinct arms tried.
evaluations.result: Figures visually report higher reward and novelty and a KL spike for the adaptive label, but no scalar table, hypothesis test, regret, recovery-time estimate, or runnable artifact is provided.
evaluations.baseline: Decaying epsilon-greedy implementation; the comparison is invalidated by fresh time-indexed Q states and unequal exploration logic.

limitations: The method is classical adaptive exploration; the quantum-field framing does not yield a distinct mathematical operator or computational advantage.
The first experiment gives the adaptive method oracle knowledge of the change point.
The printed second experiment has state-indexing and reward-construction errors that invalidate its learning interpretation.
Only a weak decaying epsilon-greedy baseline is tested; established sliding-window, discounted, change-point, UCB, Thompson, and adaptive-entropy methods are absent.
No regret bound, compute analysis, ablation, hyperparameter sensitivity, or statistically summarized recovery metric is reported.
Action-count novelty does not extend directly to large or continuous state-action spaces.
AGI, creativity, interpretability, autonomy, and quantum-hardware implications are speculative and untested.
failure_modes: Noisy Bernoulli rewards can repeatedly cross the instantaneous surprise threshold and drive unnecessary temperature oscillation.
Abrupt change that does not immediately lower sampled reward may go undetected, especially when the old action remains moderately rewarding.
High temperature can erase useful value differences and increase regret after false alarms.
Counts can reward irrelevant novelty or become meaningless under state aliasing, continuous observations, or nonstationary visitation.
A single global temperature can over-explore well-understood states while under-exploring uncertain ones.
The intrinsic bonus can conflict with external reward and create persistent unsafe or unproductive behavior.
Implementation keyed by timestep, as printed, prevents experience accumulation and reduces the purported learner to nearly memoryless sampling.
reusable_insights: Re-annealing exploration after detected distribution shift is a useful design pattern, but the detector must be evaluated without oracle change labels.
Separate the change detector, uncertainty estimator, exploration controller, and value learner so each can be ablated.
Measure dynamic regret and time-to-recovery, not just visually smoothed reward curves.
Compare adaptive exploration with matched-compute non-stationary bandit algorithms and equally informed baselines.
Treat metaphors as hypotheses generators and explicitly identify the algorithmic content that survives after terminology is removed.
Run minimal invariant tests on state keys, optimal-arm construction, and persistence before interpreting simulation plots.
open_questions: Can a calibrated change-point posterior control entropy better than thresholding single reward deviations?
Does learned state-conditional temperature improve dynamic regret over sliding-window UCB, restarted Thompson sampling, and Bayesian change detection?
How should intrinsic novelty be constrained when exploratory actions have safety costs?
Can an adaptive controller distinguish epistemic uncertainty, aleatoric noise, reward drift, and model misspecification?
Which prospective high-dimensional benchmark would falsify the claim that surprise-adaptive exploration scales beyond bandits?
Does any genuinely quantum component offer a measurable advantage over classical randomized policies for this problem?

competitive_landscape.title: Unifying Count-Based Exploration and Intrinsic Motivation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational primary work turning generalized pseudo-counts into intrinsic exploration rewards.
competitive_landscape.difference: It derives pseudo-counts from density-model learning progress and tests hard Atari exploration; the reviewed paper uses a tabular inverse-square-root action count and adds a quantum metaphor without a high-dimensional estimator.

competitive_landscape.title: Surprise-Adaptive Intrinsic Motivation for Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Earlier direct work on surprise-adaptive intrinsic motivation and entropy control.
competitive_landscape.difference: It explicitly learns to select entropy objectives online and evaluates emergent behavior in high- and low-entropy environments; this paper hand-specifies a reward-deviation temperature rule and tests only bandits.

competitive_landscape.title: Bayesian Change-Point Detection for Bandit Feedback in Non-stationary Environments
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct competitor for abrupt non-stationary bandits with autonomous change detection and restart.
competitive_landscape.difference: It couples Bayesian online change-point detection to bandit policies, proves an order sqrt(A T K_T) regret bound, and evaluates synthetic and Yahoo data; the reviewed paper uses an oracle reset or a local surprise heuristic and provides no regret analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Optimize under Non-Stationarity
competitive_landscape.relationship: Established dynamic-regret treatment of non-stationary bandit adaptation.
competitive_landscape.difference: It develops tuned sliding-window UCB and a tuning-free bandit-over-bandit framework with regret guarantees; the reviewed method compares only to decaying epsilon-greedy and does not control variation budget or regret.

competitive_landscape.title: A New Algorithm for Non-stationary Contextual Bandits: Efficient, Optimal and Parameter-free
competitive_landscape.relationship: Earlier adaptive exploration and change-detection work in non-stationary contextual bandits.
competitive_landscape.difference: Replay phases gather evidence for non-stationarity while maintaining optimal dynamic regret without hand-set variation parameters; the reviewed paper uses an unvalidated reward-surprise threshold and a global temperature.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a quantum-inspired cognitive framework that unifies reward-directed choice, intrinsic novelty, and adaptive stochastic collapse into context-sensitive 'free will' for AGI.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections 2-4 construct the analogy; Section 3 gives the softmax, count bonus, and temperature rule; Section 5 supplies bandit demonstrations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: After removing the quantum terminology, the algorithm is a familiar combination of count-based bonus, softmax exploration, and heuristic re-annealing. Surprise-adaptive entropy objectives, pseudo-count exploration, and statistically principled non-stationary bandits all predate it. The main novelty is rhetorical synthesis, while the empirical evidence is invalidated by oracle information and printed implementation errors.

reviewer_notes: Read all 22 extracted pages and line-audited both printed simulations. Primary-source searches covered pseudo-count exploration, surprise-adaptive entropy control, Bayesian change-point bandits, sliding-window UCB, and parameter-free non-stationary contextual bandits. The code-level contradictions are material: time-indexed value tables prevent learning across steps, and the constructed optimal arms do not match the prose.
